 Trump's political setback cheers global markets; Anil Singhvi explains what it means for India

Trump's political setback cheers global markets; Anil Singhvi explains what it means for India Global markets could see some relief following US President Donald Trump's political setback, as investors may expect greater checks on his policy decisions. Zee Business Managing Editor Anil Singhvi said Trump's policies had upset not just other countries but also sections of the American public, including some of his supporters.
 In his analysis, Singhvi said Trump's political setback had brought a sense of relief across global markets. He noted that people across the world, including both allies and opponents of Trump, had been concerned about his policy decisions.
 Referring to Trump's tendency to step back from some of his earlier positions, Singhvi said the American public had effectively made him "chicken out". However, he cautioned that controlling Trump's statements and public remarks would remain difficult.
 Singhvi said a strong Democratic majority would, however, act as a check on Trump's decisions and limit his ability to push through policies without opposition.
 Trump's setback: Why India could benefit 
 For India, Trump's political setback could bring some relief, particularly on trade and tariff-related issues.
 Singhvi said Trump had been particularly unhappy with India over the past two years. Against this backdrop, any reduction in pressure from Washington could be a positive development for New Delhi.
 He said Trump could adopt a relatively softer approach towards India on tariffs and the proposed trade deal. While his ego and differences with India may remain, Singhvi believes the scope for further action against the country could become limited.
 This could ease some of the uncertainty surrounding India-US trade relations. However, the extent of any relief will depend on how US trade policy evolves and how Trump responds to the changing political situation.
 Could an angry Trump trigger fresh global tensions? 
 Despite the positive market sentiment, Singhvi cautioned investors against ruling out fresh geopolitical risks.
 He compared Trump's unpredictable behaviour to the daily movements of stock prices, saying it was difficult to anticipate his next move.
 According to Singhvi, the biggest remaining concern for global markets is the possibility of Trump starting another war in response to political developments.
 He said this was one risk that investors would need to monitor closely, as it remained uncertain whether such an escalation would happen or when it could take place.
 Singhvi added that if a fresh conflict triggers a sharp correction in equity markets, investors could get another opportunity to buy stocks at lower levels.
